opportunity: mTG site-specifically attaches alkylamino-PEG (or HES) to reactive glutamines on therapeutic proteins, extending plasma half-life and stability without random chemical modification.
tg_fit: mTG as conjugation enzyme (crosslinking). Research stage; an enzymatic alternative to chemical PEGylation.

opportunity: mTG installs fluorophores, biotin, or bioorthogonal handles onto proteins at single glutamine sites for imaging, pulldown, and functional-tool creation under mild conditions.
tg_fit: mTG as labeling enzyme (crosslinking/transamidation). Research and reagent-scale tool; engineered mTG variants give high site-specificity.
evidence: An engineered mTG enables highly site-specific protein labeling, and simple mTG protocols azide- or biotin-label proteins for downstream capture.

opportunity: mTG biotinylates or tethers antibodies at the Fc glutamine so they immobilize in a uniform orientation on sensor surfaces, boosting antigen-binding capacity and assay sensitivity.
tg_fit: mTG as coupling enzyme (crosslinking). Research stage; enables oriented capture layers for immunoassays and biosensors.
evidence: Enzyme-mediated site-specific Fc biotinylation gives oriented immobilization on streptavidin surfaces with enhanced antigen-binding versus random coupling.

opportunity: Transglutaminase forms head-to-tail isopeptide bonds to cyclize peptides, improving proteolytic stability and target affinity for peptide therapeutics and display-library screening.
tg_fit: TG (microbial/tissue) as cyclization enzyme (crosslinking). Research stage; competes with polymerization side reactions.
evidence: Transglutaminase-catalyzed enzymatic cyclization produces macrocyclic peptides, and helicity-dependent TG cyclization has been demonstrated for display-selected ligands.

opportunity: TG crosslinks glutamine-lysine motifs (e.g. QLK/Q-K tags) in engineered protein polymers and self-assembling peptides to form injectable, tunable, in-situ-gelling hydrogels for delivery, biosensing scaffolds, and wound dressings.
tg_fit: mTG or TG2 as crosslinking enzyme. Research/preclinical; recombinant TG substrates allow programmable mechanics.
evidence: Modular TG-crosslinked protein-polymer hydrogels gel in situ, and TG2 self-catalytically crosslinks self-assembled collagen fibril hydrogels for wound-healing applications.

opportunity: TG2 is the dominant autoantigen in celiac disease; anti-tissue-transglutaminase IgA ELISA is the first-line, high-sensitivity/specificity screening and monitoring test worldwide.
tg_fit: TG2 used as the immobilized capture antigen in the assay (diagnostic reagent, not crosslinking). Fully commercial (marketed IVD kits, e.g. Mayo, multiple ELISA vendors).
evidence: Anti-tTG IgA by ELISA has ~95% sensitivity and >=95% specificity and is the recommended first-line celiac test at any age.

opportunity: Prophylactic IV Factor XIII concentrate replaces the missing crosslinking clotting factor, preventing life-threatening (e.g. intracranial) bleeding in congenital FXIII deficiency.
tg_fit: FXIIIa is the plasma transglutaminase; therapy SUPPLIES the crosslinking enzyme (fibrin stabilization) - not inhibition. Fully marketed (Corifact/Fibrogammin P, CSL Behring).
evidence: FDA-approved Corifact (Fibrogammin P) is an effective, well-tolerated prophylaxis dosed ~40 IU/kg every 4 weeks with no spontaneous bleeds over 52 weeks.

opportunity: Recombinant FXIII A-subunit provides an animal-plasma-free, once-monthly prophylaxis for congenital FXIII A-subunit deficiency.
tg_fit: FXIIIa transglutaminase replacement (supplies crosslinking activity, not inhibition). Marketed (Novo Nordisk, FDA-approved 2013).
evidence: FDA approved Tretten (catridecacog) in Dec 2013 for routine prophylaxis; it prevented bleeding in ~90% of patients with monthly dosing.

sector: FXIII for acquired deficiency / surgical bleeding & wound healing
opportunity: FXIII concentrate is used peri-operatively and in acquired FXIII deficiency (e.g. cardiac/major surgery, poor wound healing) to stabilize clots and reduce bleeding.
tg_fit: FXIIIa supplies fibrin-crosslinking activity (not inhibition). Clinical/off-label use beyond the congenital indication.
evidence: FXIII concentrate has been used successfully to cover surgical procedures in FXIII-deficient patients, and >20 years of pharmacovigilance support its safety.

tg_fit: TG2 as a DRUG TARGET - therapy INHIBITS transglutaminase (opposite of using mTG as glue). Clinical (Phase 2/2b; licensed to Takeda from Zedira/Dr Falk).
evidence: In a randomized Phase 2 trial ZED1227 significantly attenuated gluten-induced duodenal mucosal damage at all doses versus placebo; it is the first-in-class TG2 inhibitor in clinical evaluation.

Takeda license confirmed. Claim confirmed with phase-labeling nuance.

opportunity: Selective small-molecule TG2 inhibitors block ECM crosslinking (collagen/fibronectin) and TGF-beta-driven myofibroblast activation, reversing fibrotic remodeling in lung, heart, and kidney.
tg_fit: TG2 as a DRUG TARGET - therapy INHIBITS transglutaminase crosslinking (inverse of glue use). Preclinical across multiple organ models.
evidence: Selective TG2 inhibitors reverse the IPF myofibroblast phenotype and reduce fibronectin/TGF-beta1 deposition, and inhibitor GK921 attenuates bleomycin lung and post-MI cardiac fibrosis in mice.

sector: TG2 INHIBITION in cancer (metastasis & drug resistance)
opportunity: Blocking TG2 reverses EMT, cancer stem-cell traits, chemoresistance, and immune-microenvironment remodeling, re-sensitizing tumors (breast, ovarian, colon) to therapy.
tg_fit: TG2 as a DRUG TARGET - therapeutic strategy is INHIBITION (not crosslinking). Preclinical/research; reversible and irreversible inhibitors under development.
evidence: High tumor TG2 drives metastasis and multidrug resistance; knockdown or catalytic inhibition sensitizes cancer cells to apoptosis, with many small-molecule TG2 inhibitors reported.

Tissue transglutaminase: a new target to reverse cancer drug resistance (Amino Acids)

verification.note: Multiple peer-reviewed reviews; still preclinical.

opportunity: TG2 crosslinks aggregation-prone proteins (huntingtin, tau, amyloid-beta, alpha-synuclein); inhibiting it or blocking TG2-fibronectin interaction is proposed for Huntington's, MS, and CNS injury.
tg_fit: TG2 as a DRUG TARGET - INHIBITION approach (inverse of glue). Research/concept with mixed clinical evidence (cysteamine failed in HD).
evidence: TG2 substrates coincide with disease aggregates, but cysteamine (a non-specific TG inhibitor) failed in a randomized HD trial, so benefit in HD/AD/PD is uncertain; cell-impermeant inhibitors are proposed for MS/CNS injury.

verification.note: Strong biological rationale but mixed/negative clinical data; remains speculative.

opportunity: TG2 crosslinks ECM (collagen, fibronectin, osteopontin) and acts as a GTPase/ATPase to drive osteoblast differentiation and matrix mineralization; abnormal TG2 promotes chondrocyte hypertrophy and cartilage calcification in OA (a potential inhibition target).
tg_fit: TG2 crosslinking is required for physiologic mineralization, but pathologic OA calcification suggests INHIBITION as the therapeutic angle. Research/biology stage.
evidence: TG2-knockout chondrocytes fail to calcify while exogenous TG2 increases hypertrophy and mineralization; abnormal ECM TG2 accumulation promotes cartilage calcification linked to osteoarthritis onset.

Tissue transglutaminase (TG2) activity regulates osteoblast differentiation and mineralization in SAOS-2

verification.note: Well-supported biology; therapeutic translation (inhibition in OA) still exploratory.

opportunity: Restoring keratinocyte transglutaminase-1 (missing in TGM1-deficient lamellar ichthyosis) via topical/intradermal AAV gene therapy or enzyme-replacement cream to rebuild the skin barrier.
tg_fit: TG1 (keratinocyte TG) - therapy SUPPLIES/restores the crosslinking enzyme for cornified-envelope formation (not inhibition, not glue). Preclinical.
evidence: AAV2-TGM1 delivery increased TGM1 mRNA, protein, and enzyme activity in skin models with a favorable safety profile; topical enzyme-replacement creams are also under development.

opportunity: Plant TGs crosslink RuBisCO and cell-wall/membrane proteins and regulate photosynthesis, fertilization, senescence, and stress responses - potential targets for crop stress tolerance and yield engineering.
tg_fit: Plant TG as an endogenous crosslinking enzyme; use is exploratory (physiology/agri-biotech), distinct from mTG food/glue uses. Research/concept.
evidence: Plant TGs localize to chloroplasts, cytoplasm and cell wall, act on RuBisCO, and participate in photosynthesis, fertilization and stress responses, suggesting agri-biotech potential.

verification.note: Physiology well described; concrete biotech application is speculative and single-source.

opportunity: Rapid hemostasis and parenchymal sealing (liver, spleen, soft tissue) in dogs/cats reduce operative time and blood loss where sutures/electrocautery are impractical on friable organs.
tg_fit: Gelatin + microbial transglutaminase (+/- thrombin) forms an in-situ adhesive gel mimicking clot crosslinking; directly tested in a canine liver-trauma model achieving faster hemostasis than thrombin alone. Studied, not yet a marketed veterinary product.
evidence: A gelatin-transglutaminase-thrombin sealant significantly shortened time-to-hemostasis and controlled liver-trauma bleeding in dogs; separate in-vivo work confirmed gelatin-mTG achieves complete hemostasis in ~2.5 min in a rodent liver/femoral model.

Biomimetic sealant based on gelatin and microbial transglutaminase: an initial in vivo investigation

verification.note: Enzyme identity (mTG) and canine hemostasis efficacy confirmed in a peer-reviewed animal study; commercialization for veterinary market not yet reached.

opportunity: Large-animal (equine, bovine) field and surgical wounds involve high-flow bleeding over large deep tissue defects where fast, cheap, strongly-adhesive sealing is valuable and human fibrin sealants are costly.
tg_fit: Gelatin-mTG hemostatic dressings/sealants have been demonstrated in large-animal muscle-defect models; the low-cost non-blood-derived chemistry suits livestock economics. Applied in large-animal experiments but no dedicated marketed veterinary product identified.
evidence: Patent-documented gelatin-transglutaminase hemostatic compositions were validated in vivo in a large-animal deep muscle-defect model showing hemostasis and tissue adhesion; naturally-derived TG-crosslinked hemostatic sealants are being advanced for repairing bleeding elastic organs.

verification.note: Large-animal hemostasis demonstrated, but explicit equine/livestock clinical use is extrapolated from patent and adjacent literature.

sector: Veterinary ophthalmic corneal sealant (canine/equine melting ulcers)
opportunity: Keratomalacia (melting corneal ulcers) in horses and brachycephalic dogs progresses fast to perforation; a sutureless adhesive that seals stroma and resists collagenase would preserve vision where suturing thin cornea is difficult.
tg_fit: Gelatin-mTG bioadhesive hydrogels have been explicitly proposed and tested as ophthalmic corneal/retinal sealants in lab/animal models, and mTG-crosslinked collagen resists proteolytic degradation - attractive against melting ulcers. Veterinary-specific corneal use remains hypothetical.
evidence: Naturally-derived bioadhesive hydrogels (including gelatin-mTG chemistries) achieved sutureless repair of corneal injuries in models, and gelatin-mTG has been suggested as suitable for adhesive ophthalmic applications; no reported use in veterinary ophthalmology yet.

Disorders of the Cornea in Horses (melting ulcer clinical need)

verification.note: Strong clinical rationale and human/lab TG-corneal-adhesive evidence, but veterinary corneal application is unproven speculation.

opportunity: HA and collagen fillers degrade quickly (3-6 months) via endogenous enzymes; a covalently crosslinked, biointegrating protein filler that anchors to host ECM could give longer aesthetic correction with natural handling.
tg_fit: mTG/TG-crosslinked gelatin forms injectable in-situ gels that covalently bond to endogenous collagen, giving adhesion and localization advantages over BDDE-HA; positioned in reviews as a next-generation enzymatic crosslinking route for collagen fillers. Currently research-stage; marketed fillers still use BDDE/glutaraldehyde.
evidence: Injectable adhesive transglutaminase-gelatin gels crosslink to endogenous collagen for in-situ localization; a 2025 review flags transglutaminase among enzymatic crosslinkers for next-generation collagen fillers under physiological, catalyst-free conditions.

From Bench to Clinic: Crosslinking Approaches for Next-Generation Collagen Fillers

verification.note: TG-gelatin injectable adhesion is proven; specific approved aesthetic filler using mTG not identified - opportunity is credible but pre-commercial.

sector: Aesthetic skin biostimulation / subcutaneous ECM induction
opportunity: Beyond passive volumizing, injectable protein scaffolds that stimulate host fibroblasts to lay down new collagen/ECM ('biostimulator' fillers) offer durable skin firming and rejuvenation.
tg_fit: Enzymatically crosslinked gelatin/collagen depots present RGD motifs and a stable 3D matrix that recruit fibroblasts and induce neo-ECM; mTG is a mild physiological crosslinker well-suited to such biostimulatory injectables. Concept demonstrated with crosslinked gelatin/HA in animals; mTG-specific aesthetic use is inferential.
evidence: Subcutaneous injection of a crosslinked gelatin/hyaluronic-acid hydrogel induced production of skin extracellular matrix in vivo, supporting biostimulator behavior; enzymatically crosslinked gelatin is a low-immunogenicity, biodegradable injectable platform.

sources.title: Subcutaneous Application of a Gelatin/Hyaluronic Acid Hydrogel Induces the Production of Skin Extracellular Matrix
From Bench to Clinic: Crosslinking Approaches for Next-Generation Collagen Fillers

verification.note: Biostimulation by crosslinked gelatin/HA shown, but the cited depot used chemical (EDC) crosslinking; mTG substitution for aesthetic biostimulation is a reasonable but untested extension.

opportunity: Cornified-envelope integrity and barrier function decline with age; boosting endogenous crosslinking of envelope proteins can firm skin, reduce transepidermal water loss and improve fine-line appearance.
tg_fit: Uses endogenous epidermal transglutaminases (TG1/TG3/TG5) rather than exogenous mTG - cosmetic actives (TG-activating peptides) are designed to stimulate these enzymes to reinforce the barrier. This is an activation strategy, distinct from applying enzyme as a tissue glue; some cosmetic patents/ingredients marketed.
evidence: TGases 1 and 3 covalently crosslink cornified-envelope proteins essential for barrier function; a patented transglutaminase-activating peptide is formulated in cosmetics to reinforce barrier and stimulate epidermal differentiation.

opportunity: Onychoschizia/brittle nails affect up to 20% of adults (mostly women >50); a treatment that re-crosslinks nail-plate keratin could reduce splitting and lamellar flaking without formaldehyde-type hardeners.
tg_fit: By analogy to TG-mediated hair keratin repair, transglutaminase could crosslink applied keratin into the nail plate to strengthen it; however no direct study of TG on nails was found, so this is essentially hypothetical.
evidence: Brittle-nail reviews describe keratin fragility and the value of restoring keratin crosslinks (cystine bridges); TG-keratin bonding is proven in hair but not demonstrated in nails, so nail use is speculative.

opportunity: Lash-extension bonding is dominated by cyanoacrylates that irritate the periocular area and are not cosmetic/medical-grade approved; a gentle protein-based keratin-bonding adhesive would be safer near the eye.
tg_fit: Transglutaminase could in principle crosslink a protein/keratin adhesive to the natural lash's keratin surface, but no TG lash-adhesive product or study exists; the field is entirely cyanoacrylate-based today. Hypothetical.
evidence: Current lash-extension adhesives are cyanoacrylate-based and often not FDA-approved for cosmetic use, highlighting a safety gap; no evidence of transglutaminase being used for lash bonding.

verification.note: No TG evidence for lash adhesives; documented unmet safety need only. Pure concept, marked low/watch.

sector: Dental GBR collagen barrier membrane crosslinking
opportunity: Resorbable collagen GBR membranes degrade too fast, losing barrier function before bone regenerates; controlled crosslinking prolongs barrier life and improves mechanical handling without a second removal surgery.
tg_fit: TG2/mTG crosslink type-I collagen membranes via isopeptide bonds, improving proteolytic stability and enhancing osteoblast adhesion/proliferation; reviews rank enzymatic (mTG) crosslinking best for combined mechanical strength and biocompatibility. Research-stage for GBR membranes.
evidence: Transglutaminase-crosslinked collagen resists hydrolytic/proteolytic degradation on surfaces and promotes osteogenic differentiation; a GBR-membrane review notes mTG crosslinking gives the best comprehensive mechanical/biocompatibility performance among methods.

opportunity: Long-term composite-restoration failure stems from MMP-driven degradation of collagen in the resin-dentin hybrid layer; crosslinking the exposed dentin collagen preserves bond strength and restoration longevity.
tg_fit: Transglutaminase is one of the collagen crosslinkers applied as a dentin pretreatment to stiffen collagen and resist enzymatic breakdown at the bonded interface; evaluated within systematic reviews/network meta-analyses of dentin crosslinkers. Research/preclinical.
evidence: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of collagen crosslinkers on dentin bond strength include transglutaminase among agents (with EDC, glutaraldehyde, proanthocyanidin, riboflavin) shown to improve long-term resin-dentin bond durability.

sector: Periodontal in-situ gel / oral mucoadhesive drug-delivery patch
opportunity: Periodontitis needs local antimicrobials retained in the pocket; a mucoadhesive in-situ gel that conforms to the pocket and sustains release outperforms rinses and minimizes systemic exposure.
tg_fit: mTG-crosslinked gelatin (and gelatin-PVA / gelatin-alginate) forms mucoadhesive hydrogels with strong mucosal adhesion and prolonged intra-pocket retention and sustained drug/probiotic release. Demonstrated in oral-delivery research; not yet a marketed periodontal product.
evidence: Microbial-transglutaminase-crosslinked gelatin/PVA hydrogels were developed as oral probiotic delivery systems, and TG-crosslinked gelatin-alginate hydrogels served as sustained drug-delivery coatings, indicating suitability for mucoadhesive periodontal delivery.

opportunity: Regenerative endodontics needs injectable scaffolds that fill the root canal, retain stem cells and drive odontoblast differentiation for pulp-dentin regeneration rather than passive filling.
tg_fit: mTG-crosslinked gelatin hydrogels (incl. gelatin-GAG semi-IPNs) covalently bond via isopeptide crosslinks, provide tunable stiffness and enhance dental-pulp stem-cell osteo/odontogenic differentiation. Preclinical dental-pulp tissue-engineering research (distinct from osseointegration scaffolds).
evidence: Gelatin semi-interpenetrating hydrogels crosslinked by microbial transglutaminase enhanced the osteogenic potential of human dental pulp stem cells and promoted odontoblast differentiation with high 30-day matrix stability.

sector: Gingival / periodontal soft-tissue engineering & wound healing
opportunity: Gingival recession, periodontal defects and diabetic oral wounds heal poorly; a cell-carrying adhesive matrix that integrates with oral mucosa can accelerate epithelialization and soft-tissue regeneration.
tg_fit: mTG-crosslinked gelatin hydrogels (RGD-rich, tissue-integrating) carry stem-cell spheroids and adhesion factors, accelerating periodontal/mucosal wound closure and craniofacial repair; TG covalently bonds gelatin to host tissue amino acids. Preclinical (rodent) evidence.
evidence: Adipose-derived stem-cell spheroids in microbial-transglutaminase-crosslinked gelatin hydrogel accelerated wound closure, epithelization and keratinization in diabetic periodontal wounds and aided craniofacial defect regeneration; TG-gelatin matrices with vitronectin/fibronectin boost fibroblast proliferation.

opportunity: Denture adhesives need strong wet-mucosa adhesion with comfort and durability; current pastes wash out and give inconsistent hold.
tg_fit: mTG-crosslinked gelatin is a wet-tissue bioadhesive that bonds covalently to mucosal proteins and could function as a biologically-integrated denture/mucosal adhesive, but no denture-adhesive study using TG was found - hypothetical extrapolation from its bioadhesive mechanism.
evidence: Biomimetic gelatin-mTG tissue adhesive shows measurable increases in adhesive strength on tissue via enzymatic crosslinking, establishing the mechanism, but no evidence exists of its use as a denture adhesive.

verification.note: Bioadhesive mechanism proven, but denture-adhesive application is speculative with no direct evidence; marked low/watch.

opportunity: Root-canal sealers must seal the dentin interface durably; degradation of exposed radicular-dentin collagen undermines the seal and long-term apical closure.
tg_fit: Transglutaminase crosslinks dentin matrix (SIBLING) proteins and collagen, and could in principle stabilize the radicular dentin collagen/sealer interface; however sealers today are calcium-silicate/resin-based and no TG endodontic sealer exists. Hypothetical.
evidence: Transglutaminase is documented to crosslink SIBLING proteins in teeth (matrix stabilization), providing a biological rationale for collagen stabilization in dentin, but there is no evidence of TG use in endodontic sealers.

verification.note: Biological TG-dentin crosslinking documented, but endodontic-sealer application is pure concept; marked low/watch.

sector: Scar remodeling / scarless dermal healing (aesthetic dermatology)
opportunity: Hypertrophic scars and keloids are cosmetically disfiguring; controlling dermal collagen organization during healing can steer toward scarless repair, a major aesthetic-dermatology goal.
tg_fit: mTG-crosslinked collagen hydrogels (e.g. with bFGF) promoted scarless skin healing in vivo, but TG crosslinking also increases collagen's resistance to remodeling - a double-edged effect relevant to fibrotic scars. Preclinical; effect direction depends on formulation.
evidence: A bFGF-loaded recombinant-collagen/mTG hydrogel significantly promoted defective-skin healing with scarless outcomes in vivo; conversely, TG-mediated collagen crosslinking increases resistance to proteolytic remodeling, which can entrench fibrotic/keloid scars.

verification.note: Peer-reviewed evidence both for scarless healing and for pro-fibrotic crosslinking; net aesthetic benefit is formulation-dependent and unproven clinically.

opportunity: mTG-crosslinked gelatin (or gelatin-alginate) forms an injectable hydrogel in situ that slows diffusion of entrapped drugs/proteins for sustained/long-acting local release, offering a fibrin-clot-like enzymatic gelation without toxic chemical crosslinkers.
tg_fit: mTG already used as the gelation enzyme in research/preclinical delivery matrices; calcium-independent, mild conditions favor protein cargo.
evidence: TG-crosslinked gelatin-alginate hydrogels served as drug-delivery coatings, and TG crosslinking of gelatin retarded release of mulberry 1-deoxynojirimycin to give a prolonged hypoglycaemic effect, showing crosslink-density-tunable sustained release.

opportunity: mTG-crosslinked gelatin / gelatin-gum-arabic coacervate microspheres and microparticles give tunable, degradation-controlled release and enteric (pH-protective) delivery of drugs and nutraceuticals.
